title: Zero to Deployed — API Runway Discovery
summary: Introductory discovery focused on KiteBridge's path from prototype to first production calls. transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-10-02 16:00 UTC, Duration: 38m, Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jorge Alvarez (Redwood SE), Rina Patel (Redwood CSM) / Alex Turner (CTO, KiteBridge), Samira Khan (Product), Priya Nair (ML Eng), Owen Li (Security), Jordan (PM)

Summary (auto): Kickoff discovery to map KiteBridge's developer-first runway from prototype to production. Primary interest in fast PLG path (free credits, TTFT), with security gating for customer data and an eventual private deployment option.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — excited to meet KiteBridge. Quick intro from our side, I'm Maya, AE; Jorge is our solutions engineer; Rina handles onboarding.
[00:18] Alex (KiteBridge): Thanks Maya. We run a developer routing product, want to add contextual summarization + assistant features. Goal is to get to a working API integration fast — ideally within couple days, but we also have enterprise constraints.
[00:35] Samira (Product): Our product team cares about time-to-first-token — we wanna show PMs and early beta customers real live inference. What's realistic for a dev to go from signup to first inference?
[00:50] Jorge (Redwood SE): For most teams on hosted/redwood api, we see engineers hit first token within an hour when they follow our quickstart — 15-30 minutes for basic cURL/SDK call plus some time for schema wiring. For a full end-to-end demo with embed + chat flows, 24-48 hours if you include prompt tuning and dataset prep.
[01:12] Priya (KiteBridge): That matches our internal dev velocity, but we have to pass security bar: SSO, audit logs, and encryption. Also question about data retention and PII — do you have options for no-logging or short retention?
[01:30] Maya: Yes — hosted supports configurable retention windows; for pilot we can set shorter retention and masking. For eventual production, Dedicated or Private gives stronger guarantees and you can point to your KMS. We also integrate with SAML/SCIM for SSO and provide audit logs in the Console.
[01:48] Owen (Security): When you say KMS, do you mean we can bring our own key? We need HSM-backed keys in our cloud KMS.
[02:05] Jorge: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations for Private deployments and for Dedicated there's a marketplace KMS option — sometimes the phrasing gets fuzzy in docs, but we do support BYOK in the private offering.
[02:20] Alex: Ok good. Lay out the difference again: hosted vs dedicated vs private — we're a mid-stage startup, we prefer PLG self-serve for initial rollouts but can't expose data indefinitely.
[02:35] Maya: Short version: Hosted = fastest, pay-as-you-go with free credits, ideal for PLG. Dedicated = reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput, better isolation, SLA. Private = VPC or on-prem, full control of networking and keys. Most customers start hosted with strict retention and move to Dedicated as QPS grows or to Private for compliance.
[02:58] Jordan (PM): For the pilot, our success criteria: 1) TTFT under 48 hours for the small team, 2) 95th pct latency < 600ms for single-turn rewrite use case at 2 RPS, 3) documented security checklist. Does that seem achievable?
[03:20] Jorge: Should be achievable on hosted with a medium model and some batching turned off for latency. If latency is tighter you'll want to discuss Dedicated with pinned lower sequence-size kernels or even a quantized variant.
[03:38] Samira: Can you give rough unit economics — cost per 1K tokens for hosted vs dedicated? We need to roughly model for budgeting.
[03:50] Maya: I'll send a simple cost worksheet but high level: hosted per-token pricing is published, and Dedicated is effectively lower per-token once you hit reserved commit because of amortized GPU cost, plus options for quantized runtimes which reduce cost per token. Expect 30–60% cost savings at scale.
[04:10] Alex: Competitors we looked at were BigCloudAI (they have an integrated infra + GKE hosted thing), and we evaluated FastServe for a private runtime. The tie-breaker is developer velocity + predictable latency.
[04:27] Jorge: We're seeing customers pick Redwood when they want consistent APIs across hosted and private with good observability — metric breakdowns per token, KV cache stats, route-level latency.
[04:45] Priya: On observability — does your Console show token-level cost, per-route dashboards, and traces? We need to map to our existing tracing stack (we use LightBeat/Zipkin-ish).
[04:58] Rina (CSM): Console has route-level dashboards, per-token cost estimates, and you can stream traces to external systems via hooks. We'll share our tracing integration doc.
[05:12] Owen: About compliance — do you guys have SOC2 or ISO reports we can review? We need to show security for our board.
[05:22] Maya: Yes we have SOC 2 Type 2 and an ISO attestation; I'll attach the security packet. For Private we can also do a security deep-dive with our infra team.
[05:38] Alex: For the quickstart, how do credits work? We want to give internal devs some runway without committing.
[05:48] Maya: We offer time-limited free credits for self-serve signups; for pilots we top-up an account with targeted credits tied to an org. Credits are applied to hosted usage; if you later move to Dedicated we'll discuss credit transfer or discounted ramp.
[06:05] Samira: Can the credits be scoped to a team/org and expire automatically? We want to avoid surprise spend.
[06:12] Jorge: Yes, we can scope them and set quotas and rate limits. Also you can set hard spend caps so devs can't go over budget.
[06:26] Priya: For the samples/repo, what's the easiest stack? We use Node + serverless functions.
[06:32] Jorge: We'll share a Node SDK example and a one-click Playground template that wires up an embed+chat example. You can run locally or in your serverless.
[06:44] Jordan: Regarding model variants — can we pin to a specific model and pin a version? We need determinism for experiments.
[06:52] Maya: Yes — the platform supports version pinning and rollout policies (canary, A/B, automatic rollback). You can pin to a quantized variant for cost testing.
[07:05] Alex: We may need to do a small latency benchmark during the pilot — can you support a perf spike test?
[07:12] Jorge: Absolutely — we can run a 30-min benchmark on hosted against your target tokens and sequences. If you need sustained low latency we'll recommend a short Dedicated eval. We'll plan for a 2 RPS load and measure p95/p99.
[07:28] Priya: Any gotchas around KV cache or multi-turn context? Our use case uses a session-level KV for chat history.
[07:36] Jorge: The runtime has KV cache management — you can set TTLs, and the cache helps with repeated prefixes. For multi-turn flows it's typical to stream the KV cache and use prefix caching to reduce cost. Sometimes the transcription or docs call it K V cache and it reads oddly, but behavior is consistent.
[07:52] Alex: Network—if we start on hosted and later want private, how painful is the migration? We can't rewrite all our code.
[08:00] Maya: We design APIs to be consistent; migrations usually involve switching endpoints and reconfiguring keys. For Private, there is additional networking and firewall setup but the app-level code (API calls) remains the same.
[08:14] Samira: What are typical timelines to move from hosted pilot to Dedicated reserve? We may want Dedicated for predictable latency for 24/7 users.
[08:23] Maya: Many customers go from pilot to Dedicated within 2–3 months once usage stabilizes. Private can take longer depending on networking and compliance — think 4–8 weeks for VPC setup if everything is in place.
[08:41] Jordan: Pricing — what's the minimum commit for Dedicated?
[08:44] Maya: There are flexible tiers; we can propose a small reserved pool for a 3-month trial. I'll include pricing in the follow-up.
[08:54] Owen: Audit logs — are they integrated centrally and can we ship to our SIEM?
[09:00] Jorge: Yes, logs can be exported. We support webhook delivery and S3 export, and can integrate with common SIEMs.
[09:12] Samira: Any limitations on model sizes or sequence lengths on hosted? We sometimes run >4k token contexts.
[09:21] Jorge: Hosted supports longer sequences depending on model family; for very long contexts you may want a Dedicated node with kernels optimized for long attention. We'll flag model-family constraints in the quickstart doc.
[09:38] Alex: Ok let's talk pilot scope: 2-week hosted pilot, 90 days of credits? That seems long, maybe 30-day heavy pilot and then convert to reserved if metrics look good.
[09:52] Maya: We can do a 30–60 day pilot with targeted credits and a 2-week focused TTFT sprint. For the pilot we'll propose objectives and success metrics.
[10:05] Jordan: Success metrics again: TTFT <48h, p95 <600ms at 2 RPS, and security checklist complete.
[10:13] Maya: Noted. We'll include these as acceptance criteria in the pilot proposal.
[10:20] Samira: Anything we should prepare to make TTFT fast?
[10:24] Jorge: Yeah — onboarding checklist: 1) signup and org creation, 2) add SSO (optional), 3) generate API key, 4) run sample cURL/Node example, 5) push small prompt set and run quick latency tests. We'll attach the runbook.
[10:42] Priya: Can we get an example of a cURL call that includes streaming? We rely on streaming for UI responsiveness.
[10:48] Jorge: We'll share streaming examples — note streaming behavior and keep-alive options. Sometimes SDKs handle reconnects smoother than raw HTTP.
[11:02] Owen: Final question — if we go to Private, is there a managed option or do you expect us to operate?
[11:08] Maya: We offer both: a customer-managed on-prem package and a private managed deployment where we operate the runtime inside your VPC with strict network controls. We'll outline both options.
[11:20] Alex: Awesome. Let's wrap and recap next steps.
[11:26] Maya: Recap: Redwood will send pilot pricing and contract, SE will send quickstart runbook and sample repo, customer will provide prompt set and security requirements. We'll schedule a short perf benchmark after initial integration.
[11:40] Jordan: Sounds good — thanks all.
[11:44] Maya: Thanks everyone — talk soon.

Notes about transcription: occasional mislabels and filler words captured; acronyms sometimes transcribed oddly (SAML -> samel, KMS -> K M S).
